agenda: Reports of the Secretary-General on the Sudan and South Sudan
members: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

steps.intent: The draft aims to pressure the parties—especially the RSF—to end the Al-Fashir siege, restore humanitarian access, and reject the parallel government, while reaffirming Sudan’s sovereignty and using balanced language to avoid a Russian or Chinese veto. The most difficult points will be the generic language on external arms transfers, the rejection of the Nyala parallel authority, and accountability language, which Russia and China may seek to weaken. I expect the resolution to be able to secure at least nine votes with Western and like-minded members, while some others may abstain.

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the core objectives of the draft, including ceasefire, protection of civilians, humanitarian access and rejection of any parallel authority that undermines Sudan’s unity. Our amendments seek to preserve Sudan’s sovereignty and avoid placing the legitimate Government and the RSF on an equal footing; in particular, OP6 should target external support to the RSF and armed groups rather than constrain Sudan’s legitimate authorities. We also ask that humanitarian access be framed with respect for sovereignty and coordination with the Government, and that the political process be Sudanese-led and owned.
messages.China: China supports the Council's objective of stopping the fighting and easing the humanitarian situation in Sudan. The text should be more balanced and firmly uphold Sudan's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity and the principle of non-interference; the political process must be Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned, with regional organizations playing a leading role. We request softening unverified allegations of external support and ensuring accountability language respects Sudan's judicial sovereignty; humanitarian access should be facilitated with respect for Sudan's sovereignty.
messages.Denmark: Denmark supports the draft’s core demands for a ceasefire, protection of civilians, and immediate lifting of the siege of Al-Fashir. We ask the penholder to strengthen OP6 so that it clearly prohibits arms and military support to the parties, and OP8 so that it explicitly includes cooperation with the International Criminal Court on Darfur. We would also welcome reporting on arms transfers in OP10 and a brief South Sudan reference given the agenda item, though these are secondary to the humanitarian and accountability provisions.
messages.France: France supports the thrust of the US draft and welcomes its clear demand for a ceasefire, humanitarian access, and rejection of a parallel government. We ask the penholder to make the ceasefire demand unconditional and linked to the Personal Envoy and AU/IGAD mediation, and to strengthen OP4 and OP6 on besieged areas, cross-border access, and external military support. We can support the text with these changes; we also recall that the Council must remain seized of South Sudan.
messages.Greece: Greece supports the balanced draft and welcomes the penholder's focus on ceasefire, humanitarian access, sovereignty, and accountability. We ask that OP6 explicitly cite the Darfur arms embargo under resolution 1591 (2005), and that OP8 expressly include cooperation with the International Criminal Court regarding Darfur. These refinements would strengthen implementation and accountability while preserving the text's overall balance.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the thrust of the draft and its balanced condemnation of attacks by all parties. We would like the political process to be explicitly Sudanese-owned and African-led, and for reporting to capture external support, arms flows, and access obstacles. We also seek a reference to regional spillover, including into South Sudan, consistent with the agenda item.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the draft's core objectives: ceasefire, protection of civilians, unimpeded humanitarian access, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Sudan, and accountability. We request more balanced and verified language on external support so that the Council does not prejudge allegations or undermine respect for the sovereignty of all States. We also ask that the political process clearly affirm Sudanese ownership and the leading role of the African Union and IGAD, consistent with Pakistan's support for regional solutions. With these changes, Pakistan can support the text.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the draft’s core objectives and its focus on civilian protection and humanitarian access. We would like the text to strengthen operational language on medical neutrality, access through Adre, and due diligence against arms diversion. With these adjustments, Panama can support the draft.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the draft's core objectives, particularly on civilian protection, humanitarian access, and the rejection of a parallel government. Drawing on our experience chairing the 1591 Sanctions Committee, we ask the penholder to strengthen OP6 by demanding full compliance with the existing arms embargo and to ensure the 60-day reporting in OP10 covers arms-transfer violations and Panel of Experts information. We can support the text with these adjustments.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the draft’s core humanitarian and ceasefire objectives, but the text must not create open-ended obligations that exceed Security Council decisions or serve politicized accusations against external partners. We need OP6 reworked to focus on strict compliance with existing arms embargoes and respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, and we ask that the political process be clearly Sudanese-led and free of external interference. We also request balanced language on verified illicit arms flows and a call against unilateral coercive measures.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks the United States for the inclusive consultations and supports the draft’s core objectives. We ask for balanced language demanding that all parties, including the Sudanese Armed Forces, cease indiscriminate aerial bombardments and shelling, and for an operative paragraph on conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence. We also seek stronger language on external military support and illicit arms transfers, and affirmation of an African-led political process supported by the United Nations. These changes reflect our experience that protection of civilians, accountability, and regional ownership are essential to sustainable peace.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia thanks the United States for this draft and supports its overall direction, including the demands for a ceasefire, humanitarian access, and rejection of a parallel government. We ask for stronger operational language on accountability, including cooperation with the International Criminal Court, and a dedicated operative paragraph condemning conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence. We also encourage strengthening OP6 on arms transfers and specifying cross-border access from Chad and South Sudan in OP4. These changes would align the text with the Council's repeated commitments on protection of civilians and accountability.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft's core objectives and its clear rejection of the RSF's parallel authority and siege tactics. We ask the penholder to strengthen OP3 by demanding the immediate dissolution of the parallel structures and to add all other sieges to OP2. We also ask that OP9 anchor the political process as Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led, with the League of Arab States included, and that OP6 carry a clear international-law and Council-resolutions caveat.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports this draft as a strong basis and welcomes the penholder's focus on ending the fighting, protecting civilians, and rejecting the RSF's parallel authority. We would like OP6 strengthened to name the Darfur arms embargo and Sudan sanctions regime explicitly and to call for accountability for violations, and we ask for the Secretary-General's 60-day report to assess external arms transfers and financing. We also believe the accountability paragraph should call for cooperation with the ICC and other credible mechanisms. We can support the text with these changes.

steps.summary: The penholder incorporated core humanitarian, ceasefire, sovereignty, accountability, and reporting elements while avoiding explicit ICC language and retaining a balanced arms-transfer provision with sovereignty caveats. This should preserve P5 support and attract at least nine votes, with likely abstentions from Algeria, China, Russia, and Slovenia.

messages.Algeria: We acknowledge the penholder’s movement on OP4 and OP9, which we can support. Our red line remains OP6: the current reference to 'the parties to the conflict' continues to place the Government of Sudan and the RSF on an equal footing and risks constraining Sudan’s sovereign right to protect its people. We ask that OP6 be revised to direct the call to refrain from arms, military support and financing to the RSF and other armed groups, with an explicit affirmation that no new obligations are imposed on the Government of Sudan.
messages.China: China supports the Council's message on ceasefire, humanitarian access, and Sudan's sovereignty. However, OP6 and OP8 still contain broad language on external support and accountability that could be used to pressure Sudan or interfere in its internal affairs; these provisions should be balanced by sovereignty and judicial-sovereignty safeguards and based on verified information. We ask the penholder to adjust these provisions so that China can support the text.
messages.Denmark: Denmark supports the revised draft and welcomes the strengthened language in OP6 and the added monitoring in OP10. Our remaining priority is accountability: we ask that OP8 include a clear, carefully balanced reference to the International Criminal Court and cooperation with its independent mandate, including on Darfur. If this cannot be agreed, Denmark can support the text as a necessary humanitarian and protection response, but we will note this gap in our explanation of vote.
messages.France: France welcomes revision 1 and thanks the United States for incorporating France’s key requests on OP1, OP4 and OP6. France supports the text as it stands and calls for its adoption. We would have preferred an explicit reference to the International Criminal Court in OP8, but we will not insist and will vote in favour.
messages.Greece: Greece welcomes the explicit reference to the Darfur arms embargo in OP6 and remains broadly supportive of the text. We continue to believe that accountability for Darfur requires explicit cooperation with the International Criminal Court, consistent with resolution 1593 (2005), and ask that this be reflected in OP8. If this reference can be included, Greece is ready to support the draft.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the revised draft and welcomes the incorporation of its prior requests on arms-embargo compliance, the African-led political process, reporting on external support, and the regional dimension. To ensure humanitarian access remains principled and is not made conditional, we request one refinement in OP4: add the standard humanitarian principles language. Guyana can support the text with that amendment.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan appreciates the penholder's incorporation of our earlier points on verified reporting, sovereignty, and a Sudanese-owned process. To enable us to support the text, OP6 should be balanced and non-selective, avoiding any impression of singling out one party or validating unverified allegations of external support. We also ask that the South Sudan paragraph not call for full implementation of resolution 2781, on which Pakistan abstained; a reference to the Revitalised Agreement and relevant resolutions is more appropriate.
messages.Panama: Panama thanks the penholder for incorporating our previous requests on medical neutrality, humanitarian access, due diligence, and good offices. We regard the revised text as balanced and consistent with Panama's commitment to sovereignty, international humanitarian law, and a peaceful, civilian-led process. Panama supports the text as it stands and encourages the Council to speak with one voice.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the current text and thanks the penholder for incorporating our earlier requests on the Darfur arms embargo and reporting by the 1591 Sanctions Committee and its Panel of Experts. Our priorities remain full implementation of the sanctions regime, protection of civilians, and safe, unhindered humanitarian access, and we believe the revised draft should be put to a vote.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the draft's humanitarian and ceasefire objectives, but OP6 remains a red line: it still creates ambiguity about legitimate security cooperation with the sovereign Government of Sudan and singles out one party. We need OP6 replaced with language focused strictly on the Darfur arms embargo and non-interference, and the external-support references must be based on verified information. We also continue to insist on removing 'civilian-led' from OP9 and on a clear call against unilateral coercive measures.
messages.Sierra Leone: We thank the United States for incorporating key A3+ priorities on civilian protection, conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence, and African leadership. Sierra Leone supports the text and urges its adoption, but requests two final adjustments: explicit humanitarian principles in OP4 and a call for the resumption of the political process in OP9. These changes would strengthen balance and help ensure humanitarian access is not subordinated to any party.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia welcomes the strengthened language on conflict-related sexual violence and arms-related obligations and can support the draft. We continue to believe that accountability must be explicit: OP8 should acknowledge the role of the International Criminal Court where its jurisdiction applies, particularly regarding Darfur. We ask the penholder to add this reference; it is important but not a red line for our vote.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the revised draft as circulated. We welcome that our key concerns—demanding dissolution of parallel structures, lifting all sieges, affirming Sudanese ownership and African-led mediation including the League of Arab States, and grounding arms-transfer language in international law—have been reflected. We encourage the Council to maintain unity and speak with one voice on Sudan's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and unhindered humanitarian access.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the draft and thanks the United States for incorporating the Darfur embargo and Panel of Experts reporting. We still believe the text should explicitly name the 1591 Sudan sanctions regime and call for accountability for arms embargo violations. We also continue to push for a clear reference to cooperation with the International Criminal Court, consistent with the UK’s longstanding position on accountability in Sudan.

replies.China: partially accepted: sovereignty and verified-information language added to OP6 and external-support references, while ICC and Security Council accountability mechanisms remain in OP8
replies.Denmark: accepted: ICC reference added to OP8
replies.France: accepted: no changes requested; supports revised text
replies.Greece: accepted: ICC cooperation reference added to OP8
replies.Guyana: accepted: humanitarian principles added to OP4
replies.Pakistan: partially accepted: South Sudan reference revised and OP6 narrowed, though OP6 does not include a general 'all parties' call
replies.Panama: accepted: no changes requested; supports revised text
replies.Republic of Korea: accepted: no changes requested; sanctions and reporting priorities retained
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: OP6 red line met through narrowed Darfur/Sudan sanctions and sovereignty language; OP9 partly reflected; unilateral coercive measures call rejected
replies.Sierra Leone: accepted: OP4 humanitarian principles and OP9 'Calls for the resumption' incorporated
replies.Slovenia: accepted: ICC reference added to OP8
replies.Somalia: accepted: no changes requested; Sudanese sovereignty and African-led mediation retained
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: accepted: OP6 1556/1591 language and accountability, OP8 ICC cooperation, and OP10 recommendations incorporated

steps.summary: The revision narrows OP6 to the existing Darfur/Sudan sanctions regime with sovereignty safeguards to address Russia's red line, while adding UK and European accountability and ICC language, humanitarian principles, and stronger reporting. It is expected to pass with broad support and no vetoes, with China and Russia likely abstaining.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria generally supported recent Sudan humanitarian resolutions and its OP6 red line was partially accommodated through language affirming no new obligations on the Government of Sudan and avoiding equal treatment with the RSF. The resolution also aligns with Algeria’s emphasis on sovereignty, non-interference, rejection of a parallel government, and African-led political processes, making a favourable vote most consistent.
reasons.China: China supports the ceasefire, humanitarian access, and sovereignty provisions but retains serious concerns over the continued ICC and Security Council accountability language, which it views as inconsistent with Sudan’s judicial sovereignty and non-interference principles. An abstention signals these reservations without blocking the Council’s humanitarian focus.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark had sought a strengthened ICC reference in OP8, which the penholder accepted, and the resolution broadly aligns with Denmark’s priorities on humanitarian access, civilian protection, and accountability; Denmark therefore votes in favour.
reasons.France: France had already indicated support for the revised text, and its provisions on ceasefire, humanitarian access, sovereignty, rejection of parallel government, and accountability align with French priorities. Voting in favour reinforces Council unity on Sudan without contradicting France’s established positions.
reasons.Greece: Greece had requested stronger ICC accountability language, which was accepted, and the draft aligns with its support for humanitarian access, sovereignty, and civilian protection. As an elected member with prior favourable votes on this agenda item, Greece votes yes.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana had already signalled support with changes, and its key OP4 request was accepted; voting in favour aligns with its emphasis on humanitarian access, sovereignty and civilian protection. A brief pre-vote statement reinforces those priorities without breaking Council practice.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan’s request-based support position and the partial acceptance of its key concerns make a yes vote consistent with its emphasis on ceasefire, humanitarian access, sovereignty, and African-led mediation. The draft does not impose new sanctions and contains safeguards on verified information and non-interference.
reasons.Panama: Panama has consistently supported this agenda item’s US-penholder texts and had no outstanding requests in the final negotiation round. The draft aligns with Panama’s priorities on humanitarian access, civilian protection, sovereignty, and accountability, so it votes in favour with a brief explanation.
reasons.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea has consistently supported Security Council action on Sudan and requested no changes, and the draft aligns with its priorities on civilian protection, humanitarian access, sanctions compliance, and accountability. A pre-vote explanation reaffirms its constructive role, including as Chair of the 1591 Sanctions Committee, while making clear it will vote in favour.
reasons.Russian Federation: Russia’s red line on OP6 was addressed, so no veto was warranted, but important concerns remain over the ICC reference, the “civilian-led” political language and the rejection of the call against unilateral coercive measures, making abstention the most realistic Russian position.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone marked the draft as support_with_changes and its key requests on OP4 humanitarian principles and OP9 “Calls for the resumption” were accepted. Voting in favour is consistent with its strong record on protection of civilians, humanitarian access, sovereignty and accountability in Sudan/South Sudan.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia consistently supports Council action on Sudan focused on civilian protection, humanitarian access, and accountability, and its requested ICC reference was accepted. It would therefore vote in favour and explain its support before the vote.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia’s last negotiation position was support, and the final text retains the sovereignty protections, rejection of parallel authority, humanitarian access, and African-led mediation that are central to Somali foreign policy. As an elected Council member, Somalia would explain its favourable vote while urging compliance and regional solutions.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The UK supports the resolution because its priorities—civilian protection, humanitarian access, sanctions compliance and accountability—are reflected, consistent with its prior votes and statements on Sudan and South Sudan.
reasons.United States of America: The United States is the penholder of the draft, and its provisions reflect Washington’s stated priorities on Sudan: ceasefire, civilian protection, humanitarian access, sovereignty, accountability, and opposition to parallel governance structures. The delegation would therefore vote in favour and speak before the vote to urge Council support.

before.Algeria:
Mr. President,

Algeria will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the penholder for its engagement with our concerns, particularly with respect to paragraph 6, which now avoids placing the Government of Sudan and the Rapid Support Forces on an equal footing and affirms that nothing in that paragraph imposes new obligations on the Government of Sudan in the exercise of its sovereign right to protect its people and secure its borders in accordance with international law.

Throughout this process, Algeria has emphasized that the Council’s response must be guided by full respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and political independence, as well as the principle of non-interference in its internal affairs. We reject the establishment of any parallel authority that undermines Sudan’s unity and sovereignty. We also stress that humanitarian assistance must reach all those in need, including through cross-border and cross-line routes, while respecting Sudan’s sovereignty and in coordination with the Government of Sudan and relevant humanitarian actors.

We support an inclusive, Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led political process, with the African Union and IGAD playing a leading role in close coordination with the United Nations. We reiterate the need for a thorough and timely review of the sanctions regime, including the arms embargo, so that it does not constrain national efforts to implement security arrangements, protect civilians and build sustainable peace. We also underline that reports of illicit arms transfers and financing must be based on verified and credible information.

Algeria will continue to support all genuine efforts aimed at silencing the guns, protecting civilians and achieving a durable and inclusive peace in Sudan.
before.Denmark: Denmark will vote in favour of this resolution. We believe it sends a necessary and unified message on the need for an immediate cessation of hostilities, unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and accountability for serious violations. We welcome the inclusion of a clear reference to the International Criminal Court in OP8, consistent with the importance of cooperation with the Court and the fight against impunity. Denmark urges all parties to implement these demands without delay and remains committed to supporting African-led and United Nations efforts towards a peaceful and civilian-led political process.
before.France: France will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the United States for its efforts to produce a text that responds to the gravity of the situation in Sudan and South Sudan. The Security Council must speak clearly: the fighting must stop, civilians must be protected, and humanitarian access must be safe, rapid, unhindered and sustained, including to Al-Fashir and through the Adre and Renk crossings. France firmly rejects any parallel authority that threatens Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity. We also stress that those responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity must be held accountable, including through cooperation with the International Criminal Court. France calls on all parties to implement this resolution in full and remains fully engaged with the African Union, IGAD, the League of Arab States and the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy in support of a ceasefire and an inclusive civilian-led political process.
before.Greece: Greece votes in favour of this resolution. We welcome the inclusion of stronger language on accountability, including cooperation with the International Criminal Court with respect to Darfur, which was an important priority for my delegation. Greece remains deeply concerned by the catastrophic humanitarian situation, the continued attacks on civilians and humanitarian personnel, the siege of Al-Fashir, and the destabilizing regional dimensions of the conflict. We support the Council’s clear demand for a durable ceasefire, unimpeded humanitarian access, respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and an inclusive civilian-led political process. We also stress the need for full implementation of the Revitalised Agreement in South Sudan and for restraint amid recent tensions there. Greece will continue to support all credible efforts to end the suffering of the Sudanese people and to advance accountability and peace.
before.Guyana: Guyana thanks the United States for its efforts as penholder and welcomes the incorporation of the humanitarian principles in operative paragraph 4, a change we had requested. Guyana will vote in favour of this resolution because it sends a clear and necessary message on the immediate cessation of hostilities, the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, the lifting of the siege of Al-Fashir, and the imperative of safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access, including through the Adre and Renk crossings. We reaffirm Sudan’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity, reject the establishment of a parallel government, and call for an end to all external interference and arms flows that fuel the conflict. We also stress that accountability must be pursued, and that a peaceful, inclusive, civilian-led and Sudanese-owned political process, alongside full implementation of the Revitalised Agreement in South Sudan, remains essential.
before.Pakistan: Pakistan will vote in favour of this draft. We support the demands for an immediate ceasefire, protection of civilians and unhindered humanitarian access, as well as the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of Sudan. We appreciate the penholder’s partial incorporation of our proposals, including the narrowing of operative paragraph 6 and the revision of the South Sudan reference. At the same time, we stress that allegations of illicit arms transfers and external support must be addressed on the basis of verified information, with full respect for sovereignty and non-interference. The political process must remain Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led, with the African Union and IGAD playing a leading role in coordination with the United Nations. Pakistan’s vote reflects the humanitarian imperative and our support for de-escalation, not endorsement of any politicized or unverified claims.
before.Panama: Panama will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We remain deeply alarmed by the humanitarian catastrophe and the grave suffering of civilians across Sudan, including in Al-Fashir, and we support the Council’s demands for a durable ceasefire, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians and humanitarian personnel, full respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and accountability for serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law. We urge all parties to return to dialogue and to comply fully with their obligations under international law.
before.Republic of Korea:
The Republic of Korea thanks the United States for its penholdership and welcomes the inclusive consultations on this urgent text. The situation in Sudan requires a clear and unified message from the Security Council: all parties must immediately cease hostilities, protect civilians, and ensure safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access, including to Al-Fashir and other besieged areas. We are particularly alarmed by attacks on hospitals, markets, humanitarian personnel, and essential infrastructure, and we stress that international humanitarian law must be respected by all parties.

The Republic of Korea supports the draft’s emphasis on Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, and political independence, and its rejection of any parallel structures that undermine the unity of the country. We also underscore the importance of full compliance with the Sudan sanctions regime and the arms embargo, and, as Chair of the 1591 Sanctions Committee, we stress that reports of illicit arms transfers and financing must be addressed through verified information and credible, independent means. Accountability for serious violations, including conflict-related sexual and gender-based violence, is essential.

We further note the draft’s concern at the regional dimension of the conflict and the recent escalation in South Sudan, and we call for the full implementation of the Revitalised Agreement. For these reasons, the Republic of Korea will vote in favour of the draft resolution.
before.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation will abstain in the vote on this draft resolution. We note that a number of our principled concerns were taken into account, in particular the need to respect Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and political independence, as well as the understanding that the text must not create new obligations for the Government of Sudan. We also welcome the emphasis on a durable ceasefire, humanitarian access and a Sudanese-owned political process without external interference. However, we cannot fully support the draft in its current form. It still contains references to the International Criminal Court, a body whose work has been repeatedly politicized, and language on a “civilian-led” transition that we regard as an attempt to impose external political models. We also regret that the sponsors rejected our proposal to call for an end to unilateral coercive measures, which continue to worsen the humanitarian situation. For these reasons, we abstain, while reaffirming our support for the unity and stability of Sudan and for a peaceful settlement by the Sudanese themselves.
before.Sierra Leone: Thank you, Mr. President. Sierra Leone thanks the United States for its constructive engagement and for incorporating key concerns raised in the negotiations, including the explicit reference to humanitarian principles in operative paragraph 4 and the strengthened call in operative paragraph 9 for the resumption of an inclusive, civilian-led political process. Given the catastrophic humanitarian situation, the continuing attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and the obstruction of lifesaving assistance, the Council must speak with one voice. Sierra Leone will therefore vote in favour of this draft resolution. We urge all parties to immediately cease hostilities, lift the siege of Al-Fashir, protect civilians and medical personnel, and ensure safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access. We stress the importance of Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and political independence, and we call for accountability for serious violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law. We also support an inclusive, Sudanese-led political process with the full participation of women, youth and civil society and with the African Union and IGAD playing a leading role in coordination with the United Nations.
before.Slovenia: Slovenia will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the United States for its leadership and for incorporating our proposal to strengthen the accountability provisions, including the reference to the International Criminal Court where applicable. The Council cannot remain silent while civilians in Sudan face siege, indiscriminate attacks, starvation, sexual violence, and obstruction of humanitarian aid. We call on all parties to immediately cease hostilities, lift the siege of Al-Fashir, ensure safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access, protect civilians and humanitarian and medical personnel, and cooperate with credible accountability efforts. We also stress respect for Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity and reject any parallel structures that undermine them. We remain deeply concerned by the situation in South Sudan and call for full implementation of the Revitalised Agreement and respect for due process and human rights.
before.Somalia: Thank you, Mr. President. Somalia will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We welcome a balanced text that reaffirms the sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, and political independence of Sudan, rejects the establishment of parallel authority, and calls for an immediate ceasefire, the protection of civilians, and safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access to all people in need. We stress that the crisis in Sudan must be resolved through an inclusive, Sudanese-owned political process, with the African Union and IGAD playing a leading role, in close coordination with the United Nations and in full respect for Sudan’s sovereignty and the principle of non-interference. We also call for de-escalation and full implementation of the Revitalised Agreement in South Sudan. Somalia urges all parties to comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law and to engage in good faith with regional and international mediation efforts.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom welcomes this resolution and will vote in favour. The situation in Sudan demands an immediate cessation of hostilities, unimpeded humanitarian access, protection of civilians and accountability for violations. We are grateful that key provisions on the arms embargo, cooperation with the International Criminal Court and recommendations to strengthen compliance and accountability have been incorporated. The United Kingdom calls on all parties to implement this resolution in full.
before.United States of America: Thank you, Mr. President. The United States will vote in favour of this draft resolution. The situation in Sudan demands the Council’s urgent attention and action. This text sends a clear message that the fighting must stop, that the RSF must lift the siege of Al-Fashir, that all parties must end attacks on civilians and humanitarian personnel, and that safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access must be restored across Sudan. It also reaffirms Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity and rejects any parallel government or external interference that undermines Sudan’s unity. We call on all parties to engage in good faith with United Nations and regional mediation toward a durable ceasefire and an inclusive, civilian-led political process, and we urge all Council members to support this resolution.

after.China:
Mr. President,

China abstained in the voting on the draft resolution on Sudan just now. I would like to explain our position.

China is deeply concerned by the continued escalation of hostilities in Sudan and its severe humanitarian consequences. We support an immediate ceasefire, the protection of civilians, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and a peaceful settlement of the conflict through dialogue. We respect the sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and political independence of Sudan, and we believe that Sudan’s future and political process should be decided by the Sudanese people themselves.

The Security Council should support African-led and Sudanese-owned mediation efforts, including by the African Union and IGAD, in full respect for the principle of non-interference in internal affairs. The draft resolution just adopted still contains elements, including references to the International Criminal Court and language on political transition, that are not consistent with Sudan’s sovereignty and the realities on the ground and go beyond the Council’s proper role. Allegations concerning illicit arms transfers and external support must be based on verified information and handled with full respect for the sovereignty of all States.

China therefore abstained. We call on all parties in Sudan to de-escalate, protect civilians and humanitarian personnel, and facilitate humanitarian access. China will continue to work with the Council and regional partners to promote peace and stability in Sudan and the region.
after.Slovenia:
Mr. President,

Slovenia welcomes the adoption of this resolution. We thank the United States for its leadership and for engaging with our proposals, including on strengthening accountability and cooperation with the International Criminal Court where applicable.

Today the Council has sent a clear message: the fighting in Sudan must stop; the siege of Al-Fashir must be lifted; attacks on civilians, hospitals, schools, markets and humanitarian personnel must end; and safe, rapid, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access must be restored to all people in need. Adoption must now be followed by implementation on the ground.

Slovenia remains deeply alarmed by the catastrophic humanitarian situation, including displacement, food insecurity, disease, flooding and conflict-related sexual violence. We reaffirm Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity and political independence, and we reject any parallel structures that undermine them. At the same time, respect for sovereignty cannot shield perpetrators of international crimes. Accountability for war crimes, crimes against humanity and other serious violations is essential, including through cooperation with the International Criminal Court.

We also stress the need for de-escalation in South Sudan, full implementation of the Revitalised Agreement, and protection of political space, including for women, youth and civil society. Slovenia will continue to support the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy and regional mediation efforts, and we call on all parties to comply fully with this resolution and with international humanitarian and human rights law.

Thank you.
after.United States of America:
Thank you, Mr. President.

The United States welcomes the adoption of this resolution and thanks Council members for their constructive engagement. The Council has sent an unambiguous message: the fighting in Sudan must stop; the Rapid Support Forces must lift the siege of Al-Fashir; all parties must end attacks on civilians, hospitals, markets, and humanitarian personnel; and safe, rapid, unhindered humanitarian access must reach all Sudanese in need, including through the Adre and Renk crossings.

We reject any parallel government or authority that threatens Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity, and we call on all States to refrain from actions that fuel the conflict. The United States will work with partners to ensure this resolution is implemented, not merely noted.

We also remain deeply concerned by the recent escalation of violence in South Sudan, including in Upper Nile State, and by the charges brought against First Vice President Riek Machar. We call on South Sudan’s leaders to de-escalate, release those arbitrarily detained, and fully implement the Revitalised Agreement, including its security arrangements and preparations for credible, inclusive elections. The United States remains committed to accountability for violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law.

Thank you.
